lines: Write one real payload to a real connection in a single call, several megabytes at once.
On the other end, read it back with a far smaller buffer. How many real read calls does that actually take?
answer: This connection has no idea your write was ever one single unit to begin with.

lines: Run it for real: that one real write, received through a far smaller read buffer,
took dozens of real read calls to get back in full — confirmed directly, not assumed.
Write a message, then shut down just one direction of a real connection, for real.
Does the other side's own read call see an error now, or something else, and can that side still reply?
answer: It sees a clean end of stream, and it can still reply.
Shutting down one direction never touches the other.

lines: Run it for real: the far side genuinely saw a clean end of stream once the first side shut its own sending down,
and it could still write a real reply back, which genuinely arrived.
steps.takeaway: Half-closing just one direction of a connection leaves the other genuinely open.

lines: The real documentation describes what disabling Nagle's algorithm actually changes.
What does it say happens to small writes when that batching is left on?
answer: Held back until there's enough to send, specifically so the network isn't flooded with tiny packets.

lines: The documentation's own words: left on, small writes wait until there's enough to send,
specifically to avoid flooding the network with tiny packets — and disabling it turns that waiting off.
Separate real documentation describes what a certain closing option actually changes about closing a connection.
Does turning it on make closing behave the same, just with a timer running, or something genuinely different?
answer: Closing itself now blocks, waiting for the queue to drain or the timer to run out — which it otherwise never does.

lines: The documentation's own words: with that option on, closing won't return until everything queued has gone out, or the timer runs out.
A separate, later wait, held by the operating system itself for an entirely different reason, is something else again.
steps.takeaway: One option changes whether closing itself waits; the operating system's own wait comes after.

lines: Partial reads, a half-close that leaves one direction open, patient batching, and a closing call that waits:
these are all the same kind of surprise. A stream of bytes was never going to hand your own boundaries back.
steps.takeaway: A byte stream promises an ordered sequence of bytes, never your own write boundaries back.

lines: So, pulling this topic together: one real write of several megabytes took dozens of real reads to arrive, because this connection delivers an undifferentiated stream of bytes, not messages.
A real half-close genuinely leaves one direction open while ending the other.

Patient batching is what disabling it turns off, and a certain closing option changes whether closing itself waits — which is an entirely different thing from the operating system's own wait, held afterward, for its own reason.
